Beginners usually take a smaller size because a normal bassoon is too large: the smallest suits children, the larger ones suit bigger children or professionals. A light, narrow bassoon reed can be used, and a shorter, narrower reed helps in the high register. Most instruments have a simplified fingering system, with some alternative keys removed for reasons of space; the fingering of the upper register differs from the bassoon's, and the scale usually rises to B-flat, higher notes being possible but less reliable. Practise the simplified fingering and a quick response first, then work gradually on control in the high register.

Smaller members of the bassoon family such as the tenoroon appear in several motets by Heinrich Schütz; a Partita by Johann Caspar Frost is scored for two octave bassoons, two tenoroons, two bassoons and two horns. In the nineteenth century some argued for its use in teaching, and Jancourt often played solos on it in recitals; Berlioz imagined an ideal orchestra containing five tenoroons but never wrote for them. Today it is mostly a beginner's instrument for children in Germany and elsewhere, and it is also used by professional players.

The tenoroon is a small double-reed woodwind aerophone of the European bassoon family, classified as 422.112 in the Hornbostel–Sachs system. Its construction follows the bassoon's principle of a double reed and a tube, but it is smaller, comes commonly in F, G and E-flat, and its fingering is mostly simplified, with the keys of the upper register slightly different from the bassoon's. It is played with a lighter, narrower bassoon reed, and its tone is lighter with the reed more in evidence. It can be used by children starting out, and it can also serve as an auxiliary or independent instrument alongside the bassoon in professional performance and teaching.
